mappings.note: Recall of the symptoms Mrs Pumphrey saw. Pure information extraction, not LO-2: the item never asks what the writer means by them.
The second half, 'Is she wise in this?', is exactly the judgement that her feeding harms Tricki. Not C-E2.1-LO-1, which would only cover 'she gives him more food'.
Identifies the first-person narrator. Extraction; no character appreciation is asked, so not LO-4.
One-fact contrast of the vet's means with his client's. Not LO-4: no trait is being appreciated, only a fact retrieved.
Retrieves the treatment given (water, no food). The cause of the illness is not in question here, so not C-E2.2-LO-1.
The vet enjoying the eggs and brandy meant for the dog is the story's running joke. Not C-E2.1-LO-1: the answer is funny, not merely factual.
This is the title's irony itself -- she calls a starvation diet surgery. C-E2.2-LO-1 would miss that the question is about the misnaming, not the harm.
Asks for the narrator's character (tact, common sense). Character appreciation, not extraction.
The prediction only works if the student sees that home means renewed indulgence. Not LO-4: it is the harm, not the plot, being reasoned about.
Judges the plot's realism against life. Appreciation of plot and setting; C-E2.1-LO-2 would be wrong because no message is asked for.
The stem supplies the loneliness ('perhaps because she is lonely') and then asks whether such actions harm. Both outcomes are named in one item.
Generalises the indulgence from dog to children, which is the writer's message carried outside the text. Not LO-4.
A written personal response arguing against the pampering from the household's viewpoint. C-E2.1-LO-3 covers only length and textual support; this one takes a position.
Asks the student to defend removing the dog from the house -- the misapplied-kindness argument in the first person. Not LO-4, which would be describing Herriot rather than agreeing with him.
One-mark identification of the narrator. Extraction.
Names the vet. Extraction; no trait is asked, so not LO-4.
Retrieves her belief (malnutrition). Bare recall -- C-E2.2-LO-1 is kept for items that ask why that belief did damage.
'Only for a while' is her failure to follow the advice, which is the mechanism of the harm. Not LO-1: the point of the item is the relapse, not the fact.
Identifies the gardener. Minor-character fact, so extraction rather than LO-4.
Being unable to play ring-throw is the overfeeding's visible cost. LO-1 would treat the disabling fat as an incidental detail.
The advice (cut food, more exercise, strict diet) is the corrective to the indulgence. Not LO-1: all three options are the harm's remedy.
Lists the symptoms. Extraction.
Retrieves the vet's decision to hospitalise. Extraction.
Retrieves why the other dogs ignored him. Extraction; the surgery episode's setting is not being appreciated, so not LO-4.
Detail of the dogs' feeding habit. Extraction.
Recalls the phrase 'silky little object'. Recall of wording, not of its comic effect, so not C-E2.3-LO-1.
The staff living off the invalid's eggs, wine and brandy is the chapter's comedy. Not LO-1: the item's answer is the joke.
Retrieves why the call was made after a fortnight. Extraction.
Names the author. Bibliographic extraction; no genre or convention is involved, so not C-E2.3.
Same joke as the short-answer version: the luxuries, not affection, tempt him. Not LO-1, because the distractor 'because he loved Tricki' is what the humour defeats.
Greed is the fault the indulgence created. Not LO-1: naming greed is naming the harm's mechanism.
Her supposed diagnosis, retrieved. Same treatment as the earlier malnutrition item.
Attributes a quoted line to a speaker. Extraction.
Retrieves what was given at the clinic. Extraction.
Quantity of eggs. Extraction.
Her wailing at the parting is the dependence the writer treats sympathetically. LO-1 would make her grief a mere detail.
The 'cure' is controlling the diet, i.e. undoing the kindness that harmed him. Not LO-1, because the distractors offer real surgery and the item turns on rejecting them.
Recalls the Horlicks. A detail of the diet; the item does not ask what it did to him, so not C-E2.2-LO-1.
Recalls his favourite foods. Extraction.
Cutting the sweets is the instruction against the indulgence. Not LO-1: the item names the corrective.
Recalls the gardener's back pain. Extraction.
Recalls the coat. Extraction.
Recalls Herriot's profession. Extraction, not LO-4: no quality of his is asked for.
Recalls the fortnight's length. Extraction.
Recalls the blanket. Extraction; the comedy of the parting is not what is tested, so not C-E2.3-LO-1.
Recalls the warm box. Extraction.
Recalls water for two days. Extraction.
Recalls the rat hunting. Extraction.
Recalls the two dozen eggs a day. Extraction.
Recalls the wine. Extraction.
Names over-feeding as the real disease -- the diagnosis the whole story rests on. C-E2.1-LO-1 would reduce the central cause to a fact.
Recalls why the surgery dogs were uninterested. Extraction.
Recalls who was telephoned. Extraction.
The correct option IS 'his mistress overfed him'. This is the harm outcome stated as an MCQ, not extraction.
'Happy period' is the narrator's dry joke about living on the dog's rations. Not LO-1, because explaining the phrase means explaining the humour.
Asks what the story is an example of -- the writer's message -- and that message is that indulgence without refusal harms. Not LO-3: the demand is interpretive, not length-bound.
The goodies turning lunch into a feast for the vets is the comic subplot. Not LO-1: the item asks for the effect, which is the joke.
Pairs the advice with her refusal to take it -- the harm's mechanism in one question. Not LO-1, which the second half would leave unmapped.
Requires the inference that the pampering will resume. Not LO-4: nothing about plot or character is appreciated.

Craft question about the in-medias-res opening line. No LO covers it: C-E2.3-LO-1 is specifically the gentle humour and the title's irony, and this item is about narrative technique, so the competency is cited instead.
Transfers 'only fault' from dog to owner, which names her indulgence as the fault. Not LO-4: it is a judgement on the harm, not a character sketch.
The wailing mistress and the maids ferrying day beds and cushions is the set-piece of gentle comedy. LO-1 would list the items and miss why the scene is written that way.
Retrieves the symptoms that prompted the call. Extraction.
Builds her wealth from the servants, the wardrobe and the separate room -- character and setting. Not LO-1: the answer must be assembled, not looked up.
'She was sure he would pine and die if he did not see her every day' is her loneliness, sympathetically drawn. Not LO-1.
'Ceremonial occasion' is the narrator's mock solemnity. Not LO-1: the phrase has to be read as a joke.
Retrieves the stages of his acceptance by the gang. Extraction; the humour is not what is asked.
Retrieves the reason from the surgery scene. Extraction.
Her reading of lethargy as malnutrition and her answer of extras between meals is the harm beginning. Not LO-1: the item asks for her reasoning.
Advice plus non-compliance again, so the harm outcome rather than LO-1.
Asks what step was taken, answered by the fortnight in hospital. Extraction; the earlier 'what was the cure' item is the one that turns on the diet.
Assembles Tricki's affluent world -- setting. Not LO-1, since the evidence is spread across the text.
Asking whether the cushions are turned while the dog is critically ill is the comedy of misplaced priorities. Not LO-1.
Five-mark essay on over-indulgence towards those we care about -- the harm outcome, in the long-answer form LO-3 names.

A 120-word diary entry in which Mrs Pumphrey herself concludes her love did damage: the misapplied-kindness argument, written. Not LO-2, which would be explaining the writer's message rather than voicing it.
Asks what Tricki would say and how he would rate surgery against home -- character and setting, in long-answer form. Not C-E2.2-LO-1: the comparison is experiential, not a verdict on the harm.
A reported article setting Mrs Pumphrey's idea of care against Herriot's is exactly the argued response about misapplied kindness, in an extended written form.
'More a member of the family than a mere dog' is the substitution the loneliness produces. Not C-E2.2-LO-1: the item asks what he was to her, not what it cost him.
An explicit character sketch. Not C-E2.2-LO-1, although her indulgence features: the demand is the portrait.
The parting scene again, this time as a five-mark narration; the comedy is the substance and LO-3 the form.
Character of Herriot plus the values to emulate. Not C-E2.2-LO-3, which is about arguing the kindness point, not about admiring the vet.
The before-and-after contrast is the proof that the feeding, not disease, was the cause; it also traces the plot arc.
States the harm thesis and then asks the student to argue it out. Not LO-2: the message is given in the stem, so the work is the argument.
Extract-based multi-part: the first sub-item is retrieval from the printed passage, the rest turn on why the dog had to leave the house.
